title: Physical Properties of Food and Colloidal Systems
shortDescription: Water activity, rheology, colour and the physics of emulsions, gels and foams.
genZNote: Texture is physics you can taste. Water activity is the real boss of microbes — not 'how wet' the food looks.

sections.heading: Physical Properties
bullets: Water activity aw: ratio of vapour pressure of food to pure water; it, not total moisture, governs microbial growth — most bacteria need aw > 0.91, yeasts > 0.88, moulds > 0.80; xerophilic moulds/osmophilic yeasts down to ~0.60.
Viscosity and rheology: Newtonian (water, oil), pseudoplastic/shear-thinning (ketchup), dilatant, plastic (butter), thixotropic.
Texture attributes: hardness, adhesiveness, cohesiveness, springiness, chewiness (Texture Profile Analysis).
Colour measurement: CIE L*a*b*; density, specific heat, thermal conductivity influence processing design.
Glass transition and crystallisation matter in dried and frozen foods.

sections.heading: Colloidal Systems
sections.body: Colloids have particles ~1 nm–1 µm, scatter light (Tyndall effect), show Brownian motion and need stabilisers: emulsifiers (lecithin, mono/diglycerides) lower interfacial tension, hydrocolloids (pectin, xanthan, guar, gelatin, carrageenan, agar) thicken or gel. Instability: creaming, coalescence, flocculation, syneresis.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Physical properties such as water activity, rheology and colloidal state determine food stability, texture and processing behaviour.
keyFacts: Milk is an o/w emulsion; butter is w/o.

commonTraps: Water content and water activity are not the same.

questions.explanation: Butter has water droplets in fat.
